messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arthur is a man who has built his life on logic and order. For forty years as a database administrator, he found comfort in the predictable flow of information, in systems that behaved according to clear rules. At seventy-eight, divorced and living alone, his quiet, structured world was his sanctuary. That world shattered six months ago, not with a sudden bang, but with a creeping fire in his lungs that turned into sepsis. He remembers the initial fever, the dismissal of it as just a bad flu, and then the terrifying speed with which his breath became a shallow, useless gasp. The last clear memory before the ICU was of a paramedic’s face, etched with a grim urgency that told him everything he needed to know.

His time in the hospital is a collection of searingly vivid fragments that feel more real to him now than the memory of what he ate for breakfast. He recalls the constant, rhythmic whoosh of the ventilator that breathed for him, the slick feeling of the intubation tube down his throat, and an overwhelming, chemical smell of antiseptic that seemed to coat the inside of his nose. When these memories surface, they are not recalled so much as relived. A few weeks ago, while cleaning his bathroom with a bleach-based spray, the scent instantly transported him back to the ICU bed. For a terrifying minute, he was no longer in his sunlit apartment but back under the fluorescent lights, his chest tight, a phantom pressure in his throat making him gag. The memory is so potent, so immediate, that his present reality feels flimsy and distant in comparison, like a poorly projected film.

Since coming home, Arthur has found no peace. He had always thought of his apartment as a fortress, but he now understands the threat isn't outside. It’s inside him. He has come to see his own body as a traitor, an enemy within that could turn on him again without warning. Every cough sends a jolt of panic through him; a slight flutter in his chest is, for a moment, the beginning of the end. He is constantly on guard, monitoring his breathing, his pulse, the slightest twinge or ache. This watchfulness never ceases, not even in the perceived safety of his own home. He sits in his armchair, the television murmuring, yet every part of his attention is tuned inward, scanning for the first sign of betrayal. This internal hypervigilance leaves him perpetually exhausted, caught in a state of high alert from which there is no escape.

This experience has corroded his fundamental beliefs about the world. He was never a deeply religious man, but he held a quiet faith in a general cosmic fairness, in the idea that a good life afforded some measure of protection. Now, that faith is gone, replaced by a bitter anger. He feels he is living proof that the world is a chaotic and malevolent place where suffering is distributed at random. There is no justice, no higher power, only the cold mechanics of biology that can fail at any moment. This conviction has poisoned his relationships. When his daughter calls to check in, her gentle questions feel like an indictment of his weakness. He lashes out with a fury that shocks them both, convinced that no one can possibly understand that he is living on borrowed time in a body that has already tried to kill him.

His work, once a source of stability, has become another source of torment. He works remotely, and the low, steady hum of the server rack in his spare room, a sound he barely noticed for years, now mimics the cadence of the ICU ventilator. He finds himself getting up to unplug it, needing the silence, even though it disrupts his workflow. The intense focus required for his job is gone, shattered by intrusive memories and the constant, draining task of monitoring his own body for signs of collapse. He was referred for therapy after his daughter, tearfully, told him she couldn't bring his grandchildren to visit anymore when he was so full of rage. Arthur came not with hope, but with a desperate, exhausted feeling of having no other options. He is terrified that his fears are justified, but a small, weary part of him wonders if it might be possible to one day feel safe in his own skin again.
